name: Torsemide

angle.text: Torsemide is mentioned in depuffing circles as a strong water pill for a leaner, more defined face. It is a prescription drug for heart-failure fluid overload and has not been studied for appearance.

summary: A prescription loop diuretic for heart-failure fluid overload; mentioned in depuffing circles but never studied for appearance.
note: Prescription loop diuretic; can cause dehydration and electrolyte loss.
currentQuick:
Torsemide (torasemide) is a loop diuretic prescribed for fluid buildup from heart failure, kidney disease and liver disease.
It appears in this wiki because loop diuretics are discussed as water pills in depuffing communities. No published study has tested it for facial puffiness or any appearance purpose.
How it works: Like other loop diuretics it reduces sodium reabsorption in the kidney so more salt and water leave in the urine. Compared with furosemide it has higher oral bioavailability (about 80-90%) and a longer effect at equivalent doses.[1][5]
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include headache, increased urination, diarrhea, cough and dizziness; low potassium and hearing loss are less common. Wikipedia advises against use in pregnancy and breastfeeding. It is a prescription drug.[1]
deepLead:
Torsemide, also spelled torasemide, is a loop diuretic and sulfonamide used mainly to relieve fluid accumulation from heart failure, kidney disease and liver disease. It can be given orally or intravenously and is sold under names such as Demadex.
It was patented in 1974 and entered medical use in 1993, and it is on the WHO Essential Medicines List. Trials have compared it with furosemide in heart failure; the large TRANSFORM-HF trial reported no significant difference in all-cause mortality between the two.
No published research has examined torsemide for cosmetic purposes such as facial depuffing.

name: Hydrochlorothiazide

angle.text: Some forum users discuss hydrochlorothiazide as a daily water pill for facial puffiness. It is a common blood-pressure drug, and the appearance use rests on anecdote with no appearance studies.

summary: A common prescription thiazide diuretic for blood pressure; some forum users discuss it as a daily water pill, but it has not been studied for appearance.
note: Prescription-only; regulators have flagged non-melanoma skin cancer risk, and WADA prohibits it.
currentQuick:
Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) is a widely prescribed thiazide diuretic used for high blood pressure and fluid retention. It has been sold since 1959 and is one of the most prescribed drugs in the United States.
In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as an alternative to stronger loop diuretics for water retention. No clinical study has tested it for facial depuffing.
How it works: It blocks the sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule of the kidney, so less sodium and water are reabsorbed. Effects start within about 2 hours and last roughly 6-12 hours.[1]
Risks and caveats: Documented effects include low potassium, sodium and magnesium, high uric acid and calcium, raised blood sugar and lipids, and photosensitivity. Regulators in Australia and the US highlighted a link to non-melanoma skin cancer in 2020. It is prescription-only and prohibited by WADA.[1]
deepLead:
Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) is a thiazide diuretic used to treat high blood pressure, edema from heart failure and other conditions, and sometimes to reduce kidney stone recurrence. It became commercially available in 1959, is on the WHO Essential Medicines List, and was the 18th most prescribed drug in the US in 2024, according to Wikipedia.
It acts on the distal convoluted tubule to increase excretion of sodium and water. Commonly reported adverse effects are electrolyte disturbances, raised uric acid and blood glucose, and photosensitivity; regulators highlighted a risk of non-melanoma skin cancer in 2020.
In looksmaxxing forums, users have asked whether HCTZ is a safer daily alternative to furosemide for water retention. No published study has examined it for cosmetic purposes.

name: Chlortalidone

angle.text: Chlortalidone turns up in forum lists of possible water pills for a less puffy face. It is a long-acting blood-pressure diuretic, with no appearance data.

summary: A long-acting thiazide-like blood-pressure diuretic; a possible water pill in forum lists, with no appearance data.
note: Prescription-only; can lower potassium and sodium and raise blood sugar.
currentQuick:
Chlortalidone (also spelled chlorthalidone) is a long-acting thiazide-like diuretic and a first-line treatment for high blood pressure. It has been in medical use since 1960.
It is included in this wiki as a diuretic sometimes grouped with water pills. No study has examined it for puffiness or any appearance goal.
How it works: It blocks the sodium-chloride symporter in the distal convoluted tubule and also inhibits carbonic anhydrase. Its half-life of about 40 hours is longer than that of hydrochlorothiazide.[1]
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include low potassium and sodium, high blood sugar, dizziness, erectile dysfunction, high uric acid and photosensitivity. It is prescription-only and banned in some sports.[1]
deepLead:
Chlortalidone (chlorthalidone) is an oral thiazide-like diuretic used as a first-line treatment for hypertension and for edema from heart, liver or kidney disease. It is also used for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, renal tubular acidosis and preventing calcium kidney stones.
It was patented in 1957 and entered medical use in 1960, and it is on the WHO Essential Medicines List. It is slowly absorbed and has a half-life of around 40 hours, which Wikipedia says may explain greater blood-pressure effect compared with hydrochlorothiazide.
No published research has tested chlortalidone for facial depuffing or other cosmetic uses.

name: Indapamide

angle.text: Indapamide is a blood-pressure diuretic that is occasionally raised as a water-pill option for facial puffiness. It has large stroke-prevention trials behind it, but nothing on appearance or depuffing.

summary: A thiazide-like blood-pressure diuretic with big stroke-prevention trials behind it, but nothing on appearance or depuffing.
note: Prescription-only; monitor potassium; interacts with lithium and QT-prolonging drugs.
currentQuick:
Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic prescribed for high blood pressure and for fluid retention in heart failure. It was approved for medical use in 1977.
It is listed in this wiki as a diuretic sometimes grouped with water pills. Its trial evidence concerns blood pressure and cardiovascular outcomes, not appearance.
How it works: It acts mainly on the distal convoluted tubule to increase sodium and water excretion. Its elimination half-life is about 14-18 hours.[1]
Risks and caveats: Common effects include low potassium, fatigue and dizziness on standing. It should be avoided in sulfonamide hypersensitivity and severe kidney or liver failure, and caution is advised with lithium and QT-prolonging drugs. It is prescription-only.[1]
deepLead:
Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic used mainly for hypertension and for edema from congestive heart failure. It was patented in 1968, approved for medical use in 1977, and appears on the WHO Essential Medicines List.
Large outcome trials, including PROGRESS, ADVANCE and HYVET, tested indapamide-based regimens, often together with perindopril, in stroke survivors, people with type 2 diabetes and adults aged 80 and over. It has not been studied for cosmetic use.

name: Metolazone

angle.text: Metolazone is a potent diuretic, usually used with loop diuretics in heart failure, and it is occasionally mentioned in water-pill discussions for a drier look. No appearance data exists.

summary: A potent thiazide-like diuretic mostly used alongside loop diuretics in heart failure; no appearance data exists.
note: Strong prescription diuretic; can cause marked electrolyte depletion.
currentQuick:
Metolazone is a potent thiazide-like diuretic used for edema from heart failure, kidney disease and liver disease, and sometimes for high blood pressure. Clinicians often pair it with a loop diuretic when the loop diuretic alone is insufficient.
It appears in this wiki as a strong water pill. No study has tested it for facial puffiness or other cosmetic aims.
How it works: It blocks the sodium-chloride symporter in the distal convoluted tubule, so less sodium and water return to the blood. It remains active at lower kidney function than most thiazides and is described as about ten times as potent as hydrochlorothiazide.[1]
Risks and caveats: Fluid loss can cause low blood pressure, and electrolyte imbalances (low sodium, potassium, chloride, magnesium; high calcium and uric acid) are common concerns. Rare serious effects include aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis, pancreatitis and angioedema. It is prescription-only.[1]
deepLead:
Metolazone is a thiazide-like diuretic sold as Zaroxolyn, Zytanix, Mykrox and Metoz. It was patented in 1966 and approved for medical use in 1974. It treats edema from heart failure, kidney disease and cirrhosis and is used for hypertension, though hydrochlorothiazide is more commonly used for blood pressure.
Its characteristic role is as an add-on to loop diuretics such as furosemide to overcome diuretic resistance in heart failure. Trials of add-on strategies, including MELT-HF, have examined this use.
No published research has examined metolazone for cosmetic purposes.

name: Acetazolamide (Diamox)

angle.text: Acetazolamide is a diuretic used for glaucoma, edema and altitude sickness, and some users consider it for facial puffiness because it increases water excretion. Nothing shows it reduces facial puffiness.

summary: A sulfonamide carbonic anhydrase inhibitor used for glaucoma, edema and altitude sickness; it is a diuretic, but nothing shows it reduces facial puffiness.
note: Prescription drug with rare serious sulfonamide-type reactions; no appearance studies.
currentQuick:
Acetazolamide (Diamox) is an older prescription diuretic that blocks the enzyme carbonic anhydrase. Doctors use it for glaucoma, some forms of edema, certain seizure disorders, raised pressure inside the skull and the prevention of altitude sickness.
It is grouped under depuffing because it makes the body shed fluid, but no study has tested it for facial puffiness or any cosmetic goal.
How it works: By inhibiting carbonic anhydrase, it reduces reabsorption of bicarbonate, sodium and water in the kidney and lowers fluid production in the eye, causing mild diuresis and a metabolic acidosis.
Risks and caveats: The label lists tingling, fatigue, stomach upset, acid-base and electrolyte disturbances, and rare, sometimes fatal sulfonamide-type reactions and blood disorders. It is prescription-only in the US and carries a pregnancy caution based on animal limb defects.
deepLead:
Acetazolamide, sold under the brand name Diamox among others, is a sulfonamide-derived carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that increases the kidney's excretion of bicarbonate, sodium and water. It is an older prescription drug used for glaucoma, certain edemas, some seizure disorders and the prevention of acute mountain sickness. 
In appearance-focused communities it is listed under "depuffing" because it is a diuretic that reduces fluid in the body. The wiki found no published study that has tested acetazolamide for facial puffiness, facial water retention or any cosmetic outcome, and no community discussion of the drug was available to document. 
Its studied uses are medical: a randomized trial in acute decompensated heart failure examined it as an add-on to loop diuretics, and a trial in idiopathic intracranial hypertension examined it for protecting vision.  Labelled adverse effects include metabolic acidosis, electrolyte disturbances, paresthesia and rare, sometimes fatal sulfonamide-type reactions.

name: Triamterene

angle.text: Triamterene is a potassium-sparing diuretic, mostly paired with hydrochlorothiazide, that is occasionally mentioned in water-pill discussions. No study has tested it for facial puffiness.

summary: A potassium-sparing diuretic for edema and hypertension; no study has tested it for facial puffiness, and its label warns of fatal hyperkalemia.
note: Boxed warning for hyperkalemia; prescription-only.
currentQuick:
Triamterene is a prescription potassium-sparing diuretic, usually taken with hydrochlorothiazide, for fluid retention and high blood pressure.
It is catalogued under depuffing as a diuretic, but no research addresses facial puffiness or appearance.
How it works: It blocks sodium channels in the final part of the kidney's tubules, so more sodium and water leave in urine while potassium is retained.
Risks and caveats: The US label carries a boxed warning that high potassium can be fatal if uncorrected, especially with kidney disease, diabetes or older age. Crystal-related kidney injury and gastrointestinal and liver effects are also reported. It is prescription-only.
deepLead:
Triamterene is a potassium-sparing diuretic that blocks epithelial sodium channels in the late distal tubule and collecting duct of the kidney, increasing sodium and water excretion while limiting potassium loss. It is used for edema and hypertension, most often in a fixed combination with hydrochlorothiazide. 
It appears on the wiki under depuffing because it is a diuretic. No published study has tested triamterene for facial puffiness or any cosmetic purpose, and no community discussion of it was available to document. 
Its US label carries a boxed warning about hyperkalemia, which can be fatal if uncorrected, and triamterene has also been linked to crystal-induced kidney injury.

name: Amiloride

chain: Mild diuretic removes sodium and water
angle.text: Amiloride is a mild potassium-sparing diuretic used with other diuretics, and it is sometimes mentioned in water-retention talk. No research addresses facial puffiness.

summary: A mild potassium-sparing diuretic used with other diuretics; no research addresses facial puffiness, and hyperkalemia carries a boxed warning.
note: Boxed warning for hyperkalemia; prescription-only.
currentQuick:
Amiloride is a prescription potassium-sparing diuretic, normally added to a thiazide diuretic for heart failure or high blood pressure.
It is included under depuffing because it removes fluid, but no study has examined it for facial puffiness or appearance.
How it works: It blocks epithelial sodium channels in the distal kidney tubule, so sodium and water are excreted and potassium is retained.
Risks and caveats: The label's boxed warning says high potassium can be fatal if uncorrected, with roughly 10 percent incidence when used without another diuretic, higher in kidney disease, diabetes and older age. Minor nausea and abdominal symptoms are common. It is prescription-only.
deepLead:
Amiloride is a potassium-sparing diuretic that directly blocks epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in the distal nephron, producing a mild increase in sodium and water excretion while conserving potassium. It is used mainly alongside thiazide or other potassium-wasting diuretics in heart failure and hypertension. 
It is listed on the wiki under depuffing because it is a diuretic. No published trial has tested amiloride for facial puffiness or any appearance outcome, and no community discussion of it was available to document.
Its US label carries a boxed warning on hyperkalemia, reported in about 10 percent of patients when amiloride is used without a potassium-wasting diuretic.

name: Eplerenone

angle.text: Eplerenone is discussed on forums mainly as a costly spironolactone alternative for people wanting an aldosterone blocker, sometimes with water retention in mind. It is approved for heart failure and hypertension, with no appearance studies.

summary: A selective aldosterone blocker for heart failure and hypertension, discussed on forums mainly as a pricey spironolactone alternative; no appearance studies exist.
note: Prescription drug; hyperkalemia risk on label.
currentQuick:
Eplerenone (Inspra) is a prescription aldosterone-blocking diuretic approved for hypertension and for heart failure after a heart attack.
On looksmax.org it comes up in a couple of threads, mostly about price. No study has tested it for puffiness or appearance.
How it works: It blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor so aldosterone cannot promote sodium retention and potassium loss; it is more receptor-selective than spironolactone.
Risks and caveats: The label's main concern is hyperkalemia and raised creatinine, with higher risk in kidney disease, diabetes and with certain interacting drugs. It is prescription-only in the US.
deepLead:
Eplerenone (brand name Inspra) is a selective aldosterone receptor antagonist and potassium-sparing diuretic. The US label lists two indications: improving survival in stable adults with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction after a myocardial infarction, and treating hypertension. 
It is catalogued on the wiki as a spironolactone alternative under depuffing. Two looksmax.org threads mention it, mostly about its cost and where to obtain it; no published study has tested eplerenone for facial puffiness or other appearance outcomes. 
Its best-evidenced uses are cardiovascular: the EPHESUS and EMPHASIS-HF trials tested it in heart failure.  Labelled risks center on hyperkalemia.

name: Tolvaptan

angle.text: Tolvaptan is a prescription drug that makes the body excrete free water, and it is occasionally raised in depuffing discussion for that reason. It is approved for hyponatremia and kidney disease, with no appearance data.

summary: A prescription vasopressin blocker that makes the body excrete free water; it is approved for hyponatremia and kidney disease, with a boxed liver-injury warning and no appearance data.
note: Boxed warning for serious liver injury; requires monitoring.
currentQuick:
Tolvaptan is a prescription drug that blocks vasopressin's action in the kidney so more free water leaves in urine. It is approved for low blood sodium and for slowing polycystic kidney disease.
It appears under depuffing because of this water-excreting effect, but nobody has studied it for facial puffiness.
How it works: It antagonizes the V2 vasopressin receptor in the collecting duct, reducing cAMP and water reabsorption, an effect called aquaresis.
Risks and caveats: The Jynarque label has a boxed warning for serious, potentially fatal liver injury and warns of dehydration and abnormally high sodium. It interacts with CYP3A inhibitors and is prescription-only.
deepLead:
Tolvaptan is a selective vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist that causes aquaresis, the excretion of free water without major loss of electrolytes. It is used to treat clinically significant hyponatremia (brand Samsca) and to slow kidney function decline in adults at risk of rapidly progressing autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (brand Jynarque). 
It is listed on the wiki under depuffing because of its water-excreting effect. No published study has tested tolvaptan for facial puffiness or appearance, and no community discussion was available to document.
The Jynarque label carries a boxed warning for serious and potentially fatal liver injury, with acute liver failure requiring transplantation reported, and requires monthly liver-test monitoring early in treatment.

name: Demeclocycline

angle.text: Demeclocycline appears in de-puffing discussions because it makes the kidneys pass more free water, so some users speculate it could reduce water retention in the face. Its aquaretic effect has been studied in SIADH, and its use for facial puffiness is untested.

summary: A tetracycline antibiotic that also makes the kidneys excrete free water; nothing links it to facial puffiness.
note: Antibiotic; pregnancy and tooth-development warnings.
currentQuick:
Demeclocycline is a prescription tetracycline antibiotic. Doctors have also used it off-label to treat SIADH, because it blunts the kidney's response to antidiuretic hormone.
It is catalogued under depuffing for that water-excreting effect, but no study has tested it for facial puffiness.
How it works: As an antibiotic it blocks bacterial protein synthesis; as an aquaretic it reduces the collecting duct's response to vasopressin, increasing free water loss.
Risks and caveats: The label lists gastrointestinal upset, rare liver toxicity, sun sensitivity, and warns of fetal harm and permanent tooth discoloration in children. Antibiotic use also carries resistance and superinfection concerns. It is prescription-only.
deepLead:
Demeclocycline is a semisynthetic tetracycline antibiotic used for infections caused by susceptible organisms such as rickettsiae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Chlamydia species. Separately, it blunts the kidney's response to antidiuretic hormone, producing an aquaretic effect that has been used off-label in the syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH). 
It is listed on the wiki under depuffing because of this water-excreting effect. No published study has tested demeclocycline for facial puffiness or any appearance purpose, and no community discussion of it was available to document.
As with other tetracyclines, its label warns of fetal harm in pregnancy and permanent tooth discoloration if used during tooth development in childhood.

name: Theobromine

angle.text: Theobromine, the main xanthine in cocoa, is mentioned by users as a mild diuretic that might trim water weight and morning puffiness. Its diuretic effect is described in reference works, while its use for de-puffing the face has not been studied.

summary: Cocoa's main xanthine, a mild diuretic with no published evidence for de-puffing.
note: Diuretic classification is not backed by appearance studies.
currentQuick:
Theobromine is the main stimulant-like compound in cocoa. It is chemically close to caffeine but acts more weakly on the nervous system.
It is grouped with depuffing compounds because reference works call it a mild diuretic. No study has tested it for facial puffiness or other appearance outcomes.
How it works: It blocks adenosine receptors and weakly inhibits phosphodiesterases, with effects on blood vessels, heart and kidneys described in reference works. It is metabolised by liver CYP1A2 and CYP2E1 with a half-life of about 6 to 9 hours.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects at high intakes include sweating, tremor and headache. It is notably toxic to dogs and cats. Regulatory status is as a food ingredient in most places.
deepLead:
Theobromine is the main alkaloid of the cacao plant (Theobroma cacao) and a dimethylxanthine closely related to caffeine and theophylline. It occurs in cocoa and chocolate, with smaller amounts in tea, yerba mate, kola nut and guarana . Reference works describe it as a mild diuretic, heart stimulant and bronchodilator with much weaker central nervous system stimulation than caffeine .
In appearance-oriented discussion it is grouped with de-puffing and water-balance compounds because of its diuretic classification. No published study has tested whether theobromine reduces facial puffiness or otherwise changes appearance; the human trials that exist examined mood, cognition, blood pressure, lipids, cough and dental outcomes .
Because the amount in dietary chocolate is small and the compound is sold as a food ingredient and supplement in many places, it is not a prescription product in most jurisdictions; in South Korea it has been sold as a prescription cough ingredient .

name: Theophylline

angle.text: Theophylline was first used as a diuretic in 1902, and some de-puffing discussions cite that history as a reason to consider it for water retention in the face. It is studied and prescribed for asthma and COPD; its use for puffiness is untested.

summary: A prescription asthma bronchodilator with diuretic history; nothing tests it for puffiness.
note: Narrow therapeutic window; levels above 20 mcg/mL linked to seizures and arrhythmias.
currentQuick:
Theophylline is a prescription drug related to caffeine, used for asthma and COPD. It was first used medically as a diuretic in 1902.
It appears among de-puffing compounds because of that diuretic history. No study has tested it for facial puffiness or appearance.
How it works: It inhibits phosphodiesterases and blocks adenosine receptors, relaxing airway muscle and affecting the heart and kidneys. It is cleared by liver CYP1A2.
Risks and caveats: The US label describes a narrow safety margin: nausea, headache and insomnia at lower levels, and arrhythmias, seizures and death at high levels. Many drugs and smoking change its clearance. It is prescription-only.
deepLead:
Theophylline (1,3-dimethylxanthine) is a methylxanthine drug that inhibits phosphodiesterases and blocks adenosine receptors. It is prescribed for chronic asthma, COPD and apnea of prematurity, and occurs naturally in small amounts in tea . Its first clinical use, in 1902, was as a diuretic, before it was adopted for asthma about two decades later .
In appearance-related discussion it is listed among de-puffing compounds because of that diuretic history. No published study has tested theophylline for facial puffiness, water retention or other cosmetic outcomes. It has a narrow therapeutic window, and the US label warns that blood levels above 20 mcg/mL can cause persistent vomiting, arrhythmias and seizures that can be lethal .

name: Glycopyrrolate (oral)

angle.text: Oral glycopyrrolate is used off-label for excessive sweating, and some users take it to keep skin and clothing dry and look more composed. Its use for sweating is documented clinically, while evidence for appearance-specific use is limited.

summary: Prescription anticholinergic pill sometimes used off-label for sweating; evidence for appearance use is thin.
note: Anticholinergic effects include dry mouth, urinary retention and heat intolerance.
currentQuick:
Oral glycopyrrolate is a prescription anticholinergic. Dermatology sources list it among tablets used for excessive sweating.
Its best-documented approvals are for other conditions, and registered sweating studies of the oral form are few and small.
How it works: It blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, reducing sweat and saliva. It does not cross into the brain easily.
Risks and caveats: Dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision and reduced sweating leading to heat prostration are listed. It is prescription-only.
deepLead:
Glycopyrrolate, also called glycopyrronium bromide, is a synthetic quaternary-ammonium muscarinic anticholinergic that acts mainly outside the brain. It is given by mouth, injection, topically or by inhalation and has been used since 1961, first for peptic ulcer .
In appearance-related discussion, oral glycopyrrolate is mentioned for excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis). Reference works state that oral and topical forms have been used for gustatory and generalised sweating . The FDA's 2018 approval concerned a separate topical product, glycopyrronium tosylate, for underarm sweating . Published evidence for oral use in hyperhidrosis found here is limited to a small number of registered studies, and the injectable US label lists anaesthesia and peptic ulcer indications rather than sweating .

name: Glycopyrronium tosylate (Qbrexza)

angle.text: Qbrexza is a once-daily underarm wipe used to cut heavy underarm sweating, so users keep clothes free of sweat marks and feel more at ease in social settings. It is FDA-approved for axillary hyperhidrosis and supported by phase 3 trials.

summary: FDA-approved underarm sweat wipe with phase 3 trial support; Rx-only.
note: Anticholinergic effects; accidental eye contact can dilate pupils.
currentQuick:
Qbrexza is a once-daily prescription cloth for excessive underarm sweating, approved in the US in 2018.
Two randomised 4-week phase 3 trials found it reduced sweating more than vehicle, and a 44-week open-label study followed.
How it works: It blocks muscarinic receptors that signal sweat glands to produce sweat. Studies report limited absorption into the bloodstream.
Risks and caveats: Dry mouth and local skin reactions are described, and case reports describe pupil dilation from transfer to the eye. Prescription-only.
deepLead:
Glycopyrronium tosylate is a topical anticholinergic applied as a once-daily cloth to the underarms for primary axillary hyperhidrosis. Sold in the US as Qbrexza (2.4 percent cloth), it was approved by the FDA in June 2018 for people aged 9 and older and in Japan in January 2022 .
Its approval rests on two replicate phase 3 trials, ATMOS-1 and ATMOS-2, which compared 3.75 percent glycopyrronium tosylate with vehicle for 4 weeks and found it reduced sweating severity and production versus vehicle . A 44-week open-label extension and pediatric analyses followed .

name: Propantheline

angle.text: Propantheline is an older anticholinergic tablet that dermatology references list for excessive sweating, and users interested in staying dry and presentable look to it for that purpose. Sweat-specific trials were not found, so evidence for this use rests on reference listings.

summary: Older prescription anticholinergic tablet that dermatology sources list for sweating; no sweat trials found.
note: Dry mouth, urinary retention and blurred vision are common effects.
currentQuick:
Propantheline is an oral antimuscarinic used for stomach and bladder spasm and listed for excessive sweating.
Information on its sweat use is mostly from general references rather than dedicated trials.
How it works: It blocks acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, reducing gland secretion and smooth muscle contraction.
Risks and caveats: Fast heart rate, constipation, light sensitivity, dry mouth and urinary retention are reported. Prescription-only.
deepLead:
Propantheline bromide is an oral antimuscarinic drug that blocks acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors in smooth muscle, glands and the eye. Reference works list it for excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis), cramps or spasms of the stomach, intestines or bladder, and involuntary urination; dentists sometimes use it to reduce salivation. A brand name is Pro-Banthine .
Dermatology references group it with glycopyrrolate and oxybutynin as oral anticholinergics used for focal and generalised hyperhidrosis . The published literature found for this entry concerns mainly bladder and gastric uses; no clinical trial of propantheline for sweating was identified.

name: Aluminum chloride hexahydrate (Drysol)

angle.text: Prescription-strength aluminium chloride is used on underarms, and sometimes hands and feet, to keep skin dry and clothes free of sweat marks. Dermatology sources describe it as a first-line treatment for hyperhidrosis, and reduced sweat is visible in use.

summary: Prescription-strength antiperspirant salt; guideline first-line for hyperhidrosis, with irritation the main downside.
note: Skin irritation is common.
currentQuick:
Aluminium chloride hexahydrate is the active ingredient in prescription antiperspirants like Drysol. Guidelines cited by dermatology references list topical antiperspirants as first-line for excessive sweating.
A few small registered studies compare it with other treatments.
How it works: It is an astringent salt that reduces sweat output at the skin. Improvement is described as taking several days.
Risks and caveats: Skin irritation is the common effect. The label restricts sale to licensed practitioners. Aluminium exposure has been studied in other contexts, including a 2005 review on antiperspirants and breast cancer.
deepLead:
Aluminium chloride hexahydrate is the active ingredient in prescription-strength antiperspirants such as Drysol, used for hyperhidrosis (excessive sweating). Dermatology sources describe topical aluminium chloride as a first-line treatment, in higher concentrations than ordinary antiperspirants, which typically use aluminium chlorohydrate . It acts as an astringent that reduces sweat output .
Its most common side effect is skin irritation . The US product label found carries the statement that sale and use are restricted to a physician or licensed practitioner . Sweating is sometimes discussed in appearance culture because of visible sweat marks and odour; formal evidence comes from hyperhidrosis research.

name: Sofpironium bromide (Sofdra)

angle.text: Sofpironium bromide is a prescription underarm gel approved in Japan (2020) and the US (2024) for heavy sweating, taken up by people who want dry underarms and no sweat marks on clothing. It is an approved sweat treatment rather than a general appearance product.

summary: A prescription anticholinergic gel for underarm sweating, approved in Japan (2020) and the US (2024) - an approved sweat treatment, not a general looks product.
note: Anticholinergic: label warns of urinary retention, blurred vision and reduced sweating in hot conditions.
currentQuick:
Sofpironium bromide is a topical gel applied to the underarms to reduce sweating in people with primary axillary hyperhidrosis. It was approved in Japan in 2020 as Ecclock and in the US in 2024 as Sofdra.
Its relevance to appearance is limited to visible sweat and sweat stains. Published trials are medical studies in people diagnosed with hyperhidrosis, and no community material on it was found in the sources reviewed.
How it works: It is an anticholinergic: it blocks acetylcholine receptors (muscarinic M3) on eccrine sweat glands at the application site, which reduces the signal that triggers sweating. The US label describes it as a competitive inhibitor of acetylcholine receptors on tissues including sweat glands.
Risks and caveats: The US label lists dry mouth, blurred vision, application-site pain, redness and irritation, dilated pupils and urinary retention as the most common adverse reactions, and warns about urinary retention, lack of sweating in hot environments and transient blurred vision. It is prescription-only in the US and Japan.
deepLead:
Sofpironium bromide is a topical anticholinergic medication for primary axillary hyperhidrosis, excessive underarm sweating without an underlying medical cause. It was developed by Bodor Laboratories, licensed to Brickell Biotech (development code BBI-4000), and approved in Japan in 2020 as Ecclock and in the US in 2024 as Sofdra. 
In looks-related contexts, hyperhidrosis matters mainly for visible sweating and sweat marks on clothing. Evidence for the product comes from medical trials in patients with diagnosed hyperhidrosis; it is a prescription product, not a cosmetic or over-the-counter item. 
Phase 2 and phase 3 randomized, vehicle-controlled trials have evaluated it, and a long-term open-label study in Japan followed patients for 52 weeks. A 2025 systematic review has also assessed its efficacy and safety.

name: Zilpaterol (Zilmax)

currentQuick:
Ractopamine is a feed additive developed by Elanco that is given to pigs, cattle and turkeys in their last weeks to increase lean gain and feed efficiency. It is sold as Paylean for swine, Optaflexx for cattle and Topmax for turkeys.
It appears in appearance discussions only as a veterinary relative of clenbuterol. The sources reviewed contain no human trials of deliberate use.
How it works: It is a beta-adrenergic agonist acting on beta-1 and beta-2 receptors, and Wikipedia also describes TAAR1 agonism. In animals it increases muscle protein synthesis and fibre size and reduces fat deposition.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects in people exposed to it include rapid heart rate, tremor, headache, muscle spasm and raised blood pressure. A 2009 EFSA opinion judged the data insufficient to set a safe residue level. Welfare concerns in pigs include hyperactivity and lameness. It is permitted in the US and some other countries and banned in the EU, China and Russia.
